body.text: Kevin Rudd-era mining 'super profits' tax could have improved budget by $135b
In short:
Parliamentary Budget Office analysis commissioned by the Greens has found a mining super profits tax proposed by former PM Kevin Rudd could have raised $135 billion if it had been kept.
The proposed tax became deeply unpopular and led to Mr Rudd's removal as prime minister in 2010.
What's next?
The Greens continue to call for a tax on gas export profits, saying the public is missing out.

Labor's abandoned mining tax, which led to the 2010 toppling of then-prime minister Kevin Rudd, could have improved the budget by $135 billion if it had been kept, a Parliamentary Budget Office analysis has concluded.

Mr Rudd's proposal to tax 40 per cent of mining company "super profits" sparked a fierce $22 million industry campaign against the tax that continued until he was ousted by his then-deputy, Julia Gillard.
The unpopularity of the Resources Super Profits Tax partly prompted the leadership challenge by Ms Gillard, who replaced the super profits tax with a lighter-taxing scheme.
That was also eventually scrapped when the Coalition — under Tony Abbott — won government at the 2013 election.
Since 2012, when the super profits tax was meant to begin, the federal budget has been in deficit most years.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has warned the pressures on the budget are mounting, with borrowing costs growing and aged care and other social payments becoming more expensive, even with measures to save $38 billion over four years from the National Disability Insurance Scheme.

The federal government is also under pressure to slow down spending, as the Reserve Bank warns a lack of "domestic capacity" is driving up inflation, alongside international pressures including the war in Iran.
The Greens have called for a 25 per cent tax on gas export profits and an increase in the rent tax levied on offshore petroleum companies, saying both could help to fund the budget.
Senator Steph Hodgins-May said the PBO modelling showed the missed opportunity by not pursuing revenue from the resources giants.

"We were interested to see what other revenue has been lost as a consequence of our government not being willing to stare down those big gas exporters, those big resources industry players, to make them pay what they owe," the senator said.
"They jump with fright as soon as there are a couple of billboards at the airport warning them off going after these profits.

"We're sick of the government telling us we can't have nice things, nice essential things, like free early childhood education, like wiping HECS debt, like having a well-funded National Disability Insurance Scheme, and being told those things aren't possible when they are leaving in the realm of $135 billion on the table because they are unwilling to stare down a few mining and gas corporations."

"Our focus is on getting more gas available to Australians at affordable prices. I'm not aware of any policy where you put a tax of that magnitude on a product that would make it more affordable to everyday Australians," she said.
The government has previously warned a gas export tax could also damage Australia's relationships with Asia, which depends on Australian gas, and which Australia depends on for petrol and diesel.

The PBO suggested the mining tax would have raised a net $24 billion last financial year if it had been kept, which would have eliminated the government's $22.3 billion budget deficit, with all else being equal.

It found over the 14 years that the tax would have operated, it could have improved the overall budget position by $135 billion — assuming that the major reform would not impact mining company behaviour.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers, who was a senior adviser to then-treasurer Wayne Swan when the resources super profits tax was introduced, declined to comment.
But the ABC was told the government was not considering reinstating the resource rent tax.
Modelling assumes no impact to mining production or investment

The $135 billion budget windfall paints an optimistic picture of the mining tax's impact, with the Parliamentary Budget Office assuming that taxing 40 per cent of super profits "would not have changed mining company behaviour regarding the level of resource production and investment or mineral prices".
But mining companies warned the super profits tax would have put some projects back on the shelf and driven future investment offshore, with consequences for the entire economy.

At a Senate inquiry into the proposed gas export tax held earlier this year, Shell Australia chair Cecile Wake said it would be economically damaging, and a similar windfall tax in the United Kingdom had caused a contraction of industry there.

"The UK offshore operators forecast for the period of 2025–2029 shows a decline in investment from 14.1 billion pounds [$26.6 billion] per annum at the time it was introduced down to 2.3 billion pounds per annum over that forward estimate," Ms Wake told the inquiry.
Senator Hodgins-May said the industry was recycling old warnings.

"The fact we are hearing the same playbook from killing [the resources super profits tax] to killing a gas tax tells you everything you need to know. They roll out the same talking points regardless of the reforms that are on the table," she said.
The 2010 Henry Tax Review recommended replacing mining royalty payments on production with a broad "rent" tax, saying that would encourage more marginal mining companies and further exploration.
Mr Henry maintained his support for a resources profit tax at the senate inquiry into a gas export tax earlier this year.

"Just do it, in the national interest, just do it, and stop the crap that the Australian public have put up with for decades now in respect of taxation of Australia's finite resources," Mr Henry said in April.

While the mining tax was ultimately scrapped, a separate resource rent tax on offshore petroleum products has existed for decades, at a rate of 40 per cent of taxable profits, after accounting for exploration and other costs.

The Petroleum Resource Rent Tax was tightened by the federal government in 2024 to cap deductions for gas extractors and bring forward the payments they make, which has collected an additional $1.2 billion since those reforms were introduced.
